messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Marisol is a 39-year-old detective who came to treatment after years of telling herself that what happened in her childhood should not still have such force over her. She grew up in a small apartment where nights could turn suddenly volatile. The scene she returns to most often is not a full narrative but a set of sharp images: her mother backed against the kitchen counter, her father looming close, the muscles in his neck slick with sweat, his voice exploding through the room, a hand reaching out too fast. Even now, what comes back to Marisol is visual and immediate—the shine on his skin, the angle of her mother’s face, the blur of movement as he grabbed and shoved. When she tries to remember the event on purpose, to put it in order and explain exactly what happened from beginning to end, she finds that she cannot get hold of it that way. Instead there are pictures, and with them a crushing grief that can leave her feeling winded.

As a child she learned to stay very still and read the room quickly. Years later, she is highly respected in her police work for noticing exits, positioning, and changes in other people’s bodies before anyone else does, but in her private life the same vigilance feels relentless. In restaurants she cannot simply sit down; she scans first and chooses the seat that feels most protected, usually one with a wall behind her and a clear view of the door. If someone moves unexpectedly near her, especially from the side, her whole body reacts before she can think, as if danger is already upon her. At night she wakes abruptly and checks her surroundings to make sure she is safe. She knows she is in her own home with her partner, yet she still sits up, listens, looks toward the bedroom doorway, and waits for the jolt in her chest to settle.

Certain moments at work can undo her composure with humiliating speed. When a suspect or witness raises his voice during an interview, she feels the old alarm flood her body. The smell of sweat in a cramped interrogation room or hallway can be even worse, bringing back those childhood images with no warning. She does not describe this as “remembering” in an ordinary sense; it feels more like being seized by fragments she cannot control. Physical touch is also difficult. If a colleague brushes past her in a narrow space or places a hand on her shoulder without warning, she stiffens or recoils. Her partner has learned that even affectionate contact can be met with withdrawal. Marisol avoids being touched whenever she can, and over time this has changed the texture of the relationship. She still cares deeply for her partner, but she has narrowed the range of closeness she can tolerate and says she often feels absent even when they are together.

Over the years she has tried to solve the problem by shutting down feeling altogether. She avoids not only things that might upset her, but also things that might stir any strong feeling at all, positive or negative. She keeps herself busy, stays flat, leaves gatherings early, and prefers the structure of work to the unpredictability of emotional intimacy. On the worst nights, when the images of her mother’s face and the sound of shouting will not leave her alone, she has hurt herself physically to stop thinking. She describes this without drama, more as something she discovered “worked” in the moment by cutting through the internal noise.

What troubles Marisol almost as much as the symptoms themselves is what she has come to believe they say about her. She is frightened that these reactions mean she is going crazy. She also doubts her own judgment in ways that are painful for someone in her profession; despite years of competent investigative work, she can become certain she cannot trust herself to do the right thing. Beneath that is a more private conviction she has rarely said out loud: that what happened in her home had something to do with the sort of person she is. The belief is not logical, and she knows that, but it persists with the same emotional certainty as the nighttime fear.

She finally sought help after a recent case involving a loud domestic disturbance. In the apartment, a man shouted from another room and moved suddenly toward the doorway while she caught the heavy smell of body odour in the heat. She reacted instantly, more startled than she felt she should have been, and later at home she could not settle, waking repeatedly to check that the house was secure. Her partner, who had been asking her for months to talk to someone, told her he was worried not only about how on edge she seemed but about how small their life had become around what she was trying not to feel. Marisol came in saying she wanted to understand why childhood scenes she can barely deliberately recall still arrive with such force. What frightens her most is the idea that she is losing her mind; what she hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to sleep through the night, sit beside the person she loves without bracing, and move through her work without every shout or sudden movement feeling like the beginning of the same night all over again.
